name: Jimmy Caputo
title: Agentic Engineering Platforms
abstract: What does a platform need when AI agents start writing code, running tests, and shipping changes? This talk looks at how engineering platforms can give agents the context, tools, and guardrails they need to work effectively. Jimmy will discuss how developer workflows, observability, and platform design can help teams adopt agents while keeping engineers in control.

Previously Director of Product Management at Datadog, he worked on Cloud Cost Management and integrations. He holds degrees in mechanical engineering from Stanford University.

name: Arjun Iyer
title: Agents Write the Code. The Platform Has to Prove It Works.
abstract:
Coding agents have made writing code cheap. They haven't made shipping it faster.

That's because the bottleneck has moved to verification. Before a change ships, it has to run in an environment that looks like production to prove it works. Most teams have a handful of these environments, built for the pace of human developers. Add agents, and changes either pile up waiting their turn or ship without being properly tested. Either way, the productivity gains don't show up in delivery.

That makes environments the constraint, and platform teams the ones who can fix it. In this talk, I'll share what we've learned working with engineering teams to give every change its own environment, at the speed agents work.

You'll leave knowing:

- How to spot where your environments will break as agent output grows
- How to evaluate environment approaches on cost, speed, and scale
- How to give agents environments of their own, so they test changes before opening a PR and reviewers get work that's already verified
bio: Arjun Iyer is the CEO and Co-founder of Signadot. Signadot helps engineering teams verify code before it merges, at the volume coding agents now produce it. He holds an MS in Computer Science from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

name: Gaurav Vashisht
title: Measuring the Exact ROI of AI : A Framework for Quantifying the Return on Agentic AI Investments
abstract: Measuring AI usage is easy. Measuring AI's true business value, quantifiable and tangible is the hard part. This article lays out a three part framework that closes that gap: observe the manual baseline, reconstruct the real effort, penalize rework. If your board is asking what the AI budget returned, this is for you.
bio: Gaurav Vashisht is an Enterprise Systems and AI leader with 22+ years of experience building and supporting financial infrastructure for global organizations. name: Felipe Sanz
title: The Exam Moved to Monday: Agent Memory That Knows What to Forget
abstract:
Most agent memory starts as an append-only log: embed what the user said, store it, retrieve the nearest matches later. Then a student tells their AI tutor the midterm is Thursday, and a week later says it moved to Monday. Both facts are now in the vector store, and similarity search has no way to know the second cancels the first.
This talk walks through the long-term memory I designed and built for an AI tutor used by university students. Every extracted fact ends in one of four operations: add, update, delete, or ignore. Vector similarity only finds the closest existing memory. A small LLM picks the operation, because embeddings show that two sentences concern the same exam and say nothing about which is still true.
I'll cover the rest of the pipeline too: a cheap router that skips the nine turns in ten with nothing worth remembering, six education-specific memory categories, twenty recalled candidates reranked to five, and a chat that keeps answering when memory fails. I'll also cover the failure modes this design brings, including two data stores written without a transaction and background writes that a deploy can drop.
You'll leave with the four-operation merge loop and a checklist of failure modes for your own memory layer.
bio: Felipe Sanz is the founder of [New Premise](https://newpremise.ai/), an Austin consultancy that helps companies put AI to work one department at a time and measures the result in return on investment. Before New Premise, he designed and built the long-term memory system and the evaluation process for an AI tutor used by university students, following three and a half years at Celonis building machine learning for the global go-to-market organization. Felipe has also volunteered with Austin AI Hub, building AI tools for nonprofits that fight human trafficking, and guest lectured on advanced databases at IE University. He writes about AI at felipe-sanz.com.

name: Gordon Worley
title: Automating Maintenance with AI
abstract: You have a constant stream of maintenance signals: logs, metrics, CVEs, and, of course, Sentry alerts. Unfortunately, it quickly becomes more than any one human can triage, so stuff gets dropped on the floor. That's where AI can help. I'll show you how I'm using bots to automate dozens of maintenance tasks every week so the team can stay on top of the pile and get back to shipping features.

name: Byron Ellis
title: Preventing a Software Dark Age
abstract: As organizations adopt agentic engineering, planning, iteration, and PR reviews are all occurring via agents without much in the way of visibility. Architectural decisions and design context are moving transient AI session transcripts rather than durable engineering artifacts that have been the foundation of developing reliable software. It’s not that the work of design and review isn’t happening, it’s that we’re in a dark age where the record of it is deleted due to a 30 day retention policy because unlike traditional SDLC artifacts we can’t be sure it doesn’t contain sensitive data. In this talk we’ll cover some ideas on how we as an industry can start to dig into this session data not only to understand ROI but also perhaps to generate new durable artifacts that actually let us produce more reliable software than we could before.
bio: Byron recently joined Faros.ai with the suitably ambiguous title “Member of Technical Staff” to build tools that help organizations fully adopt agentic development practices after going through the process first hand. He came to Faros.ai from Linked in where he was a Principal Staff Engineer at LinkedIn where he focused on large scale Data Infrastructure projects. Prior to that he spent time in Google Cloud on the BigQuery and Dataflow teams as well as YouTube where he spent several years working on Trust and Safety infrastructure.

name: Prasad M K
title: Your Logs Vanished and Nothing Errored: Three Ways Kubernetes Drops Logs Silently
abstract: Kubernetes loses container logs in three ways that never reach the application: kubelet rotation lag under heavy writes, disk-pressure eviction that deletes a pod's log directory, and a race between rotation and the log shipper's read cycle. Each one is documented in Kubernetes and Fluent Bit issue trackers (#110630, #134324, #10414), but nobody ties them together. I'll show how application-level sequence markers make these gaps visible, and how to classify each gap by cause using kubelet events and node conditions. Attendees leave with the settings to tune and a simple way to detect loss in their own pipelines.
bio: Prasad M.K. is a Cloud Solution Architect and Full Stack SRE with 25+ years of experience engineering high-availability systems for Fortune 500 accounts. He specializes in Kubernetes, large-scale data pipelines (Kafka/Pulsar), and agentic AI architectures on AWS Bedrock. Prasad is the author of DAY ONE AI and regularly publishes research on AI agent governance and system design.

name: Lakshmi Mamidala
title: From Reactive Ops to Audit-Ready Flow: Architecting Continuous Compliance & Secure AI Governance
abstract:
As enterprise platforms scale, the friction between developer velocity and security compliance creates massive bottlenecks. You can no longer afford to treat vulnerability management, CVE remediation, and regulatory audits (like NIST 800-53 or CMMC) as manual processes. Furthermore, as organizations rapidly integrate AI engines, traditional security guardrails are failing to keep up with autonomous workloads.
Drawing from enterprise-scale architectural patterns, this session explores how to shift compliance from a blocker to a built-in feature. We will break down how to automate continuous compliance and fleet-wide patching without disrupting uptime. Finally, we will look at the next frontier of platform reliability: designing secure governance layers and containment frameworks for AI-driven operations.
Key Takeaways
Automating the Audit: Design continuous compliance pipelines that enforce regulatory readiness automatically.
Zero-Downtime Remediation: Architectural strategies for automated CVE patching in mission-critical environments.
The AI Governance Blueprint: Vendor-neutral frameworks for securing AI workloads and establishing agent containment.
bio: Lakshmi Mamidala is a Technical Architect and Product Strategist specializing in Enterprise Cloud Reliability, FinOps, and Secure AI Governance for highly regulated systems. She leads the product vision and architectural design for mission-critical enterprise platforms, transforming complex infrastructure into scalable, automated solutions. Her work focuses on building AI-driven architectures that enable autonomous self-healing, optimize enterprise cloud economics, and enforce continuous regulatory compliance at scale. As an active industry voice, Lakshmi also serves as a technical expert and advisor for early-stage AI startups and autonomous technology research initiatives.

name: Sergey Sergeev
title: From Agent Chaos to Voice-Driven Flow: Building a Self-Improving Knowledge Management Suite
abstract:
A year ago my “AI-assisted” workflow was still manual: open five coding agents, chase which session owned which task, paste context by hand, and discover merge conflicts only when something already hurt. The agents were smart; the *system* was not. I kept losing the plot between ideation, implementation, and “wait, who has the worktree?”
So I built the coordination layer I wished existed—and then I made the suite run itself. What started as a personal knowledge board became a voice-driven dashboard with automated implementers that claim work, track sessions, and keep a living queue. Auto-ideation surfaces the next cuts. A “merge doctor” watches for conflict and repair cases instead of letting mid-merge worktrees become archaeology. When an implementation stack needs a human, it doesn’t wait for me to refresh a browser—it reaches me on the voice terminal I’m already using.
The interesting part isn’t any single feature. It’s the before/after: from fragmented agent babysitting to a self-optimizing loop where every painful failure—stale pulls, stuck claims, silent merge flakes—becomes a product requirement the next day. The tool improves the workflow; the workflow feeds the tool.
In twenty-five minutes I’ll walk the architecture as lived experience: what broke, what we automated, where humans still belong, and what I’d change if I were demoing this to strangers instead of myself. Bring scars and opinions—I want both.
bio: Sergey Sergeev is a Senior Staff Engineering Architect for Observability for AI at Splunk (Cisco). He holds two US patents and has 20+ years building high-scale distributed data systems.

name: Marcello Golfieri & Lin She
title: Let the Job Survive: Fault-Tolerant GPU Training Without the 3am Page
abstract:
Meta's Llama 3 team logged 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days of training on 16,384 GPUs, about one every three hours, and roughly 78% traced back to hardware. For the platform team, every one of those is the same drill: a page, a dead job, a restart from the last checkpoint, and hours of recomputed work nobody gets back.
This talk is about breaking that loop. We walk through three techniques from our Clockwork playbook. First, link-level failover inside NCCL: when a NIC, optic or cable flaps, traffic moves to the node's surviving NICs and fails back when the link recovers, with no job restart. Second, live GPU migration: moving a worker off a degrading or to-be-patched node onto a spare, triggered by an ordinary Kubernetes taint or Slurm DRAIN, and resuming at the same iteration, again without any training-code changes (for these two, we have a demo to show). Third, multi-node platform snapshots: capturing a running distributed job in under 20 seconds with no training-code changes (sneak peek, since we are launching this in 6 weeks).
We will cover what each one costs to run, where it falls back to plain checkpoint-restart, and what changes in your runbooks and on-call rotation.
bio: *[Marcello Golfieri](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marcellogolfieri/)* is driving Customer Success at Clockwork.io, harvesting signals from the field and feeding them back into the product line. Previously at AWS in Strategic Accounts, he enjoys Contract Bridge and learning new foreign languages, so that he can travel disguised as a local (well, most of the time…) *[Lin She](https://www.linkedin.com/in/linshe/)*is a Software Engineer at Clockwork.io working on fault-tolerant distributed GPU training. He integrated TorchPass into Megatron-LM and TorchTitan, and runs the chaos clusters that hit it with thousands of injected GPU and network failures. Before AI infrastructure, he spent a decade running SkyPixel, a Minecraft platform he grew past a million users.

name: Manu Gurudatha
title: Hurdles for Adoption of AI Across Incident Management
abstract: Everyone building AI into incident management assumes the hard part is the model and accuracy: better anomaly detection, smarter correlation, more reliable auto-remediation. Having spent years watching how teams actually adopt (or stall on) this technology, including our own at PagerDuty, I've found the technology is rarely the blocker. This talk looks at the real, recurring patterns that stall AI adoption in incident response: getting customers to start using it long enough for a positive reinforcing loop to take hold, organizations bolting AI onto a process that was never consistent enough to automate in the first place, cost overruns that erode trust in the ROI, and the harder problem of telling AI-created incidents apart from human-created ones. Even with high-quality signals and a clear value proposition, these remain the true blockers to adoption. This isn't a technical deep dive, it's a product and organizational lens on a problem I'm actively working through: what separates teams that successfully bring AI into their incident workflow from teams that stall out after the pilot. Expect real patterns, some surprising ones, and an honest look at what's still unsolved.
bio: Manu Gurudatha is a VP of Engineering at PagerDuty, where he drives the Incident Management, AIOps, CSOps, Status Pages that power PagerDuty's end-to-end customer journeys. With his previous experiences, Manu has a proven track record of building strong products and platforms, sometimes from scratch and scaling those to sustain performance for thousands of customers.

name: YuZhao Zhang
title: Terraform MCP server: Four real-world AI infrastructure patterns
abstract:
Based on my published https://www.hashicorp.com/en/blog/terraform-mcp-server-four-real-world-ai-infrastructure-patterns
What if AI agents could do more than generate Terraform code? What if they could understand your organization's infrastructure standards, automate workflows, and enforce governance while improving developer productivity?
In this session, we'll explore how the Terraform MCP Server connects AI agents with trusted infrastructure context through four practical patterns: no-code infrastructure workflows, self-service provisioning using Private Module Registry, policy enforcement with Sentinel or OPA, and infrastructure orchestration at scale with Terraform Stacks.
Through real-world scenarios, you'll discover how platform engineering teams can leverage Agentic AI to simplify infrastructure operations, accelerate delivery, and maintain security and compliance. Walk away with practical ideas for evolving your platform from traditional Infrastructure as Code toward intelligent, governed, AI-assisted infrastructure automation.

She specializes in platform engineering, Terraform, and Agentic AI, with a focus on helping enterprises adopt emerging technologies. name: Matthew Senick
title: Ship Meaning With the Data: CI/CD for Semantic Layers and Agent Assets
abstract: Data teams have mature CI/CD for transformations, but the context agents rely on to use that data rarely gets the same treatment. Metric definitions, relationships, and instructions usually live in hand-edited semantic layers that drift the moment a model changes. This talk shows how to deploy that context with the data, shipping dbt models, semantic objects like Sigma data models and Snowflake semantic views, and agent assets like Cortex Agents and Sigma agents as a single release. Each change is versioned in one repo, validated in CI, gated by agent evals, and promoted together through every environment. You’ll leave with a reference pipeline and a playbook for making “agent-ready” a deploy gate, not an afterthought.

name: Roy Derks
title: Agent Sandboxes Are the Missing Runtime for AI
abstract: AI agents are no longer just calling APIs. They're writing code, executing commands, browsing the web, and interacting with entire systems. But giving agents more autonomy also introduces new risks. How do you let an agent execute arbitrary code without exposing your infrastructure, credentials, or sensitive data? That's where agent sandboxes come in. In this talk, we'll explore why isolated execution environments are becoming a critical part of the agentic AI stack, how technologies like containers and microVMs enable secure execution, and how to architect agents that can safely run code, use tools, and interact with real-world systems.
bio: Roy Derks is a Dutch software developer, author, and IBM developer-experience specialist focused on making AI agents more reliable through better tools.

name: Arunkumar Mathiyazhagan
title: Ghost APIs — Why Your Deprecated Endpoints Are an Attacker's Best Friend
abstract:
Every API team deprecates endpoints, but almost none fully kill the traffic. Across complex distributed systems, deprecated endpoints frequently remain reachable long after documentation is removed—creating a sprawling, invisible attack surface hiding in plain sight. We call these Ghost APIs.
In this session, I will walk through how to identify, measure, and systematically eliminate that attack surface—developing a security pattern that establishes a secure-by-default reference standard across distributed services. Attendees will learn:
- How Ghost APIs form and why they persist even in mature, well-governed API platforms.
- A practical playbook for API deprecation that combines continuous traffic analytics, client outreach, and secure-by-default interceptors.
- How to build deprecation hygiene into your CI/CD pipeline so Ghost APIs never accumulate again.
bio: Senior Software Engineer at AWS Athena with 16+ years of experience leading teams and architecting hyperscaler-scale distributed systems serving 30k TPS across 35 AWS regions. Deep technical expertise in low-level memory and IO optimization, serverless compute platforms (Firecracker microVMs), and Java/Python/Go/Rust distributed microservices. Recognized for delivering re:Invent launches end-to-end.

name: An Phan
title: Your Platform Users Aren't Always Software Engineers
abstract: We often talk about internal platforms as products for software developers: golden paths, self-service infrastructure, deployment workflows, and abstractions over Kubernetes and the cloud. But what happens when your users are ML scientists and domain experts, and the systems they build eventually interact with the physical world? As a Data Infrastructure Engineer working on robotics and AI systems, I've found that many platform engineering ideas still apply, but the interface changes. A good platform isn't just infrastructure hidden behind an API. It gives people enough autonomy to move quickly without requiring them to understand every system underneath it. In this talk, I'll share what I've learned building internal data and ML infrastructure for users outside traditional software engineering. We'll look at where self-service helps, where abstractions leak, how platform teams can create leverage across specialized teams, and why the best internal platform may be the one its users barely realize they're using.
bio: An Phan is a Senior Data Infrastructure Engineer at Hippo Harvest, where he builds data and ML infrastructure for robotics and AI systems operating in the physical world. His background spans software engineering, data infrastructure, industrial AI, and machine learning systems across agriculture, manufacturing, semiconductors, and connected devices. He is particularly interested in how infrastructure can create leverage for ML scientists, domain experts, and other engineers without requiring everyone to become an infrastructure expert.

name: Mark Pawlikowski
title: Kill It and Watch It Come Back: Hands-on with Reliaburger
abstract:
I have never run a Kubernetes cluster. Yes, I said it.
Are you still with me? Cool!
Over the past last five years I talked to thousands of SREs and platform engineers at the conferences I run with my team: [SREday](https://sreday.com/), [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), [PLATFORMday](https://platformday.com/) and [Conf42](https://www.conf42.com/). The same story keeps coming back. Before the first container hits production you step into the world of Kubernetes, and then you need to build a whole team just to keep it running. A killjoy for many smaller teams. We started talking with my brother, [Miko Pawlikowski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mikolajpawlikowski/), how we could help the community ease some of these pains. Miko has been running platform teams on Kubernetes for 10+ years, leading him to start writing Reliaburger: one Rust binary with the scheduler, gossip, Raft, eBPF service discovery, ingress, mTLS, registry, metrics, logs, GitOps and chaos testing inside, driven by TOML. An app with health checks, ingress and autoscaling is twelve lines. He wrote the software. I am here to hand it to the community and see what you do with it.
This is a hands-on session, so bring a laptop (macOS on Apple silicon or Linux; Windows is not supported yet).
In 30 minutes you will:
1. Install Reliaburger with one command and start a node on your laptop. No container runtime, no root, no VMs: the built-in process runtime runs plain binaries.
2. Deploy an app from a twelve-line TOML file and watch it in the terminal dashboard and the web UI.
3. Ship a deliberately sick version and watch the health checker restart it, then roll back with one command.
4. Break it on purpose with the built-in fault injector: kill an instance, freeze another, and let `relish wtf` explain what just happened.
5. Read the manual and the source code from inside the binary, so you can keep going after the session.
6. Tell us what broke and what you liked.
Reliaburger is free and open source (Apache 2.0), and it is version 0.1, so it will break. That is where you come in. We are looking for helpers, burger ambassadors and contributors: people who will run it, break it, file the issues, write the docs and tell their teams. There are millions of practitioners running parts of Kubernetes they do not need, with more people than they should need to run it. We want this to become a community-driven project, just as our conferences are.
bio: Mark Pawlikowski runs SREday, LLMday and PLATFORMday, in-person conferences for the people who keep production up, and Conf42 online. He is not an engineer. He has spent the last five years listening to SREs and platform engineers describe what their work is actually like, and now brings Reliaburger, his brother Miko's batteries-included container orchestrator, to that community to play with, break and build on.

name: Gabe Gramajo
title: Beyond the AI Demo: Building Automation That Works in the Real World
abstract:
An AI demo can impress in five minutes. Making it work reliably inside a business takes much more. Drawing on 18+ years of IT delivery and his work building AI solutions for small and midsize businesses, Gabriel “Gabe” Gramajo shares a practical approach to connecting AI with the systems, workflows, and people that keep a business running.
Using examples from hospitality and professional services, this session explores how to turn everyday problems - missed inquiries, repetitive data entry, and disconnected applications - into focused automation opportunities. We’ll cover choosing the right first use case, connecting existing platforms, designing human handoffs, and measuring results beyond the number of conversations an AI handles.
Attendees will learn how to:
* Identify automation opportunities with clear business value.
* Design integrations with permissions, failure handling, and human oversight.
* Build reusable capabilities while accommodating each customer’s workflows.
* Measure success through time saved, completion rates, customer experience, and revenue captured.
Designed for founders, product leaders, and technical teams moving AI from experimentation into daily operations.

Through Ideas Factory, Gabe develops practical AI solutions for small and midsize businesses, combining enterprise delivery experience with an entrepreneur’s understanding of everyday challenges. name: Ryan Doherty
title: Operational Excellence
abstract: Operational excellence isn't a monitoring problem. It's a human one, and it lives "above the line" in the people, processes, habits and priorities that no logging, metrics or alerting setup can replace. Drawing on over a decade of amateur endurance racing, where a team with an ordinary car eventually won through disciplined operations, this talk shows how development relates to operations as building a race car relates to winning a season.
bio: Ryan is a vocal site reliability engineer who loves learning from incidents and attempting to answer the question "are we resilient?". He's been a frontend engineer, backend engineer, operations engineer, site reliability engineer and everything in between. Part time amateur race car driver too.

name: Gaston Acosta Ramas
title: The Glue Is the Platform: Why Most Production Errors Live Between Teams
abstract:
Platform teams measure what they own: cluster health, pipeline success, uptime. But the incidents that hurt most rarely start inside a team. They start between teams. An alert pages the wrong people. A golden path gets bypassed because it’s slower. A ticket bounces between queues for three days.
Drawing on 15 years leading platform and SRE organizations at Apple, Zipline, WeWork and Rivian–Volkswagen, this talk argues that the interface between infrastructure and application teams is the platform, and that it deserves the same rigor as your Kubernetes clusters. Through real incident stories, you’ll see the three seams where production errors most often originate, and the specific changes that closed them.
You’ll leave with a five-question diagnostic to find the seams in your own org, and a practical playbook for fixing them without a reorg.
bio: Gaston Acosta Ramas is an engineering leader with more than 15 years running platform, SRE and infrastructure organizations. He has been a founding CTO, Head of Cloud Infrastructure at Zipline, SRE leader for Apple Intelligence’s Private Cloud Compute, and a manager of managers at WeWork, and has led platform work at Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies. He has migrated organizations of more than 200 engineers onto platforms he built. Working towards international credentialing in coaching, he now advises engineering leaders on reliability, platform strategy and the team dynamics that make them work.

name: Hariharan Subramanian
title: Beyond the Sunset: Real-World Lessons Migrating from Ingress-NGINX to Kubernetes Gateway API at Scale
abstract:
Migrating production edge traffic from legacy Ingress controllers (like ingress-nginx) to Envoy-based implementations of the Kubernetes Gateway API is rarely as simple as running an automated manifest converter. The real challenge lies in bridging subtle behavioral gaps—unsupported annotation hacks, different timeout models, and altered connection-pooling semantics—without causing downtime or localized outages.
This talk shares production-tested patterns for orchestrating a zero-downtime, safe migration across multi-cluster environments using an external, health-driven traffic steering strategy. Attendees will learn:
Dual-Plane Traffic Steering & Dynamic Probing: How to decouple legacy and modern ingress planes behind weighted external DNS and global traffic directors, turning migration into an incremental canary rather than a high-risk cutover.
Telemetry-Driven Health Probing: Why standard endpoint liveness checks fail during ingress migrations, and how to wire synthetic health-probe endpoints directly to proxy-level downstream metrics (e.g., Envoy /stats downstream connection and handshake error thresholds) to automatically gate traffic based on true downstream health.
Quorum-Based Automatic Rollbacks: How to implement a fleet quorum threshold across ingress proxy replicas—automatically flipping the global canary back to the legacy plane the moment partial replica failure occurs, preventing zombie instances from serving errors.
The DNS Caching Dilemma: The operational reality of DNS-based routing: handling aggressive client-side caching, calculating cost/query load trade-offs when temporarily dropping TTLs (e.g., from 300s to 30s), and safely stepping TTLs back up once cutover stabilizes.
The "Broken Annotations" Trap: Practical strategies for mapping bespoke NGINX annotations, snippet rewrites, and authentication hooks into native Gateway API resources and extension filters.
bio: Hariharan Subramanian is a Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft working on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), specializing in large-scale cloud infrastructure, scalability, and secure distributed systems. With over 16 years of industry experience across health, retail, and cloud infrastructure, he brings deep, hands-on production expertise to complex platform transitions. Hariharan is an active contributor and reviewer for the open-source Envoy Gateway project, focusing on modern ingress architectures, Kubernetes Gateway API adoption, and secure service-to-service communication with Istio.

name: Sujoy Datta Choudhury
title: Agent Config Is Platform Config
abstract:
I broke my own agent twice in one week. Once by hand: I renamed a profile file and the agent came up with the old name. The frontmatter wins. Once with a language model: I asked it for a strict code-review agent, and it returned clean YAML that parsed on every line and invented two fields the schema does not have. Reading it carefully, I flagged a third field as invented. That one was legitimate. The machine hallucinated two fields, the human reviewing it hallucinated a third, and neither of us is a schema.
An agent profile is platform config. It decides which tools the agent may call, which model answers, and which MCP servers it reaches. Generating that configuration got automated. Checking it did not. This talk is about the review gate I built to close that gap in CLI Agent Orchestrator (CAO), an open-source project that coordinates multiple AI coding CLIs as a team of specialist agents, each defined by a profile. I will start with what CAO is and why it runs existing CLIs as full processes with their own authentication instead of replacing them. Then I will walk through the self-service profile authoring surface I contributed across eleven merged PRs: a CLI, discovery, a validation API, guarded write endpoints, and a web UI. The UI checks the schema at save time, previews the final document as you type, and clones with the frontmatter name rewritten so a copy cannot keep its source's identity. The honest part: seven rounds of maintainer review, mostly async races, pinned down with around 290 tests.
You will leave with a paved-road pattern for any config an LLM writes for you, agent or otherwise: a schema the tool enforces, findings in plain words, and a wrong file that fails at save time in front of its author instead of at run time inside an agent that looks like it is working.
bio: Sujoy Datta Choudhury is a Software Architect with 20+ years of experience in distributed systems, AI platforms, and cloud infrastructure. As Technical Architect at Amazon Ads, he oversees platforms processing billions of daily requests and $1.1B+ in ad volume. Previously VP at BlackRock, he built mission-critical Fintech platforms and founded their global AI hackathon. An AWS Labs maintainer and published researcher, he holds an M.S. in Data Science.

name: Sujeeth Pasham
title: Green Builds, Red Dashboards: Building Platforms That Catch Release Failures Early
abstract: A green pipeline and a completed deployment do not guarantee a healthy service. Many production outages begin with engineering decisions that each look reasonable: a flaky test rerun until it passes, a feature flag assumed to stop all related work, a canary judged healthy on overall metrics, or a rollback plan never tested against newly written data. When these gaps live in the shared delivery platform, every team that ships through it inherits them. This session follows an illustrative release from first commit to production recovery. At each stage, it shows where platform-owned systems such as CI pipelines, test infrastructure, flag services, progressive delivery, and deployment tooling can let failures slip through. Three deeper walkthroughs explain why a disabled flag can leave background processing running, why a healthy canary can hide an unhealthy customer cohort, and why restoring a previous binary may not restore service once data or configuration has changed. Each scenario connects a hidden assumption to its customer impact and to a safeguard platform teams can build into their golden paths. These include quarantining flaky tests with visibility, flag kill switches verified end to end, canary analysis that checks each customer cohort, and compatibility checks across version and configuration changes. Attendees will leave with a release-safety checklist for their own CI/CD and deployment tooling, along with patterns that make safe releases the default path for product teams. They will also gain a practical method for testing not only whether software works, but how systems behave as they move between versions, configurations, and recovery states.
bio: Sujeeth Reddy Pasham is a Senior Software Engineer with over a decade of experience designing and building scalable, distributed cloud systems. Currently at Microsoft, he works on Azure Entra and Microsoft Graph, leading the development of Multi-Tenant Organizations and Cross-Tenant Sync solutions that enable secure, seamless collaboration across customer tenants. The architects distributed APIs, scalable data models, and resilient cloud services that support millions of users while maintaining high availability and performance. Previously at Amazon Web Services, Sujeeth contributed to Amazon S3 Glacier, where he designed and optimized large-scale data retrieval systems for enterprise customers. He developed asynchronous and byte-range retrieval capabilities that significantly reduced retrieval time and cost, improved billing accuracy, and enhanced system scalability and operational stability. His work supported highly durable storage systems while ensuring strong security and compliance standards. Earlier, at Oracle Cerner, he built analytics and access management solutions that improved application performance and streamlined administrative workflows. Throughout his career, Sujeeth has driven improvements in reliability, observability, and deployment automation, consistently achieving high service availability. He is passionate about solving complex engineering challenges, mentoring teams, and delivering cloud solutions that create measurable business impact.
